vignette: As a paramedic, Lena had seen her fair share of traumatic events, but none had left an indelible mark on her life like the police violence she experienced three years ago. The memory of that fateful night still felt like it was happening in real-time - the sound of sirens, the feeling of being pinned to the ground, and the pain of her wrists being twisted behind her back. When she tried to recount the events to friends or family, she would get tangled in a web of confusion, unable to put the memories in order or finish her sentences. This disjointedness only added to Lena's growing sense of unease. She had started to feel like she was constantly on edge, scanning her surroundings for potential dangers and seeking out safe seats wherever she went - always with her back against a wall and an escape route in mind. Even the slightest unexpected touch would send her heart racing, as if her body was primed to respond to threats at all times. These physical reactions were a constant reminder that her memories of that night were still very much alive. As a result, Lena had developed a set of coping mechanisms to deal with these feelings of threat and vulnerability. She avoided anything that reminded her of the person who had harmed her - from avoiding certain neighborhoods to steering clear of people in authority or uniform. She also suppressed any anger she felt, convinced that allowing herself to express it would only lead to more trouble. At work, this meant biting her tongue when dealing with difficult patients or colleagues, even if it meant sacrificing her own emotional well-being. These avoidance strategies had become so ingrained that Lena barely noticed them anymore - until they started to interfere with her daily life. She found herself turning down shifts that involved working with police officers, and avoiding social gatherings where she might encounter people in uniform. Her friends and family were starting to notice the changes in her too, commenting on how withdrawn and isolated she had become. Lena's attempts to manage her memories of the traumatic event only seemed to perpetuate a vicious cycle. By suppressing her emotions and avoiding reminders of that night, she felt like she was holding onto the past rather than letting go. Her memories remained frozen in time, still capable of evoking a visceral response whenever they resurfaced. The more she tried to push them away, the more they seemed to dominate her thoughts and feelings. As Lena struggled to come to terms with her experiences, she began to realize that she couldn't keep living like this. Her relationships were suffering, her job was becoming increasingly stressful, and she felt like she was losing herself in the process. It was only when she hit rock bottom - after a particularly grueling shift where she had snapped at a colleague for no reason - that Lena finally decided to seek help. She knew it wouldn't be easy, but she was desperate to break free from the cycle of fear and avoidance that had been holding her hostage for so long.
